subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} {subject} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: Describe motion using position, velocity and acceleration
Velocity as the rate of change of position; acceleration as the rate of change of velocity
Displacement as the change in position
Average and instantaneous velocity, speed and acceleration, and how to find them
Use the four equations for uniformly accelerated motion
Motion with constant and with changing acceleration
Projectiles without fluid resistance: treat the horizontal and vertical motions separately
How fluid resistance changes a projectile's flight

questions.q: The position x of a body moving along a straight line is recorded at intervals of 1.0 s, starting at t = 0: x = 0, 5.0 m, 8.0 m, 9.0 m, 8.0 m, 5.0 m and 0. Which statement about the motion of the body is correct?
options: The acceleration is zero at t = 3.0 s, because the body is momentarily at rest at that time.
The acceleration is negative up to t = 3.0 s, then positive as the body speeds up again.
The acceleration is constant and negative; the body reverses direction at t = 3.0 s.
The acceleration decreases while the body slows down, then increases as it speeds up.
optionWhy: A student who thinks zero velocity means zero acceleration picks this. The velocity is zero for only an instant at t = 3.0 s, and it is still changing at the same rate (−2.0 m s⁻¹ each second) through that instant, so the acceleration there is −2.0 m s⁻², not zero.

A student who reads 'speeding up' as a positive acceleration picks this. The changes in position fall by the same 2.0 m each second throughout, so the acceleration stays −2.0 m s⁻². After t = 3.0 s the velocity is negative and the acceleration is negative, so the body speeds up in the negative direction.

The change in position each second is +5.0 m, +3.0 m, +1.0 m, −1.0 m, −3.0 m, −5.0 m: the velocity falls by 2.0 m s⁻¹ every second, so the acceleration is a constant −2.0 m s⁻². The velocity changes sign between the 3rd and 4th second, at t = 3.0 s, where x is greatest, so the body reverses direction there.

A student who links the size of the acceleration to the speed picks this. The speed falls and then rises, but the velocity changes by the same −2.0 m s⁻¹ in every second, so the acceleration is constant throughout.
questions.explain: The change in position each second is +5.0 m, +3.0 m, +1.0 m, −1.0 m, −3.0 m, −5.0 m: the velocity falls by 2.0 m s⁻¹ every second, so the acceleration is a constant −2.0 m s⁻². The velocity changes sign between the 3rd and 4th second, at t = 3.0 s, where x is greatest, so the body reverses direction there.
questions.working: Changes in position over successive 1.0 s intervals: +5.0, +3.0, +1.0, −1.0, −3.0, −5.0 m, so the average velocities are +5.0, +3.0, +1.0, −1.0, −3.0, −5.0 m s⁻¹. Each is 2.0 m s⁻¹ less than the one before, so the acceleration is constant at −2.0 m s⁻². The velocity passes through zero at t = 3.0 s (where x = 9.0 m is greatest): the body reverses direction there while its acceleration stays −2.0 m s⁻².

questions.q: The graph shows how the velocity of a car varies with time during the first 10 s of its motion along a straight road. What is the displacement of the car during these 10 s?
optionWhy: A student who uses distance = speed × time with the final speed, 20 m s⁻¹ × 10 s, picks this. The car is only at 20 m s⁻¹ from 4.0 s onwards; during the first 4.0 s it is slower, so the displacement is less than 200 m.

A student who takes the average velocity to be (u + v)/2 = (0 + 20)/2 = 10 m s⁻¹ for the whole 10 s picks this. That formula applies only to uniform acceleration; here the acceleration is not uniform over the 10 s, and the area under the graph must be used.

Displacement is the area between the velocity–time graph and the time axis: a triangle of area ½ × 4.0 × 20 = 40 m for the first 4.0 s, plus a rectangle of area 6.0 × 20 = 120 m for the next 6.0 s, giving 160 m.

A student who confuses the two graph operations finds the gradient, (20 − 0)/(10 − 0) = 2.0, and reports it as a displacement. The gradient of a velocity–time graph is an acceleration (units m s⁻²); the displacement is the area under the graph.
questions.explain: Displacement is the area between the velocity–time graph and the time axis: a triangle of area ½ × 4.0 × 20 = 40 m for the first 4.0 s, plus a rectangle of area 6.0 × 20 = 120 m for the next 6.0 s, giving 160 m.
questions.working: Displacement = area under the velocity–time graph. Triangle from 0 to 4.0 s: ½ × 4.0 s × 20 m s⁻¹ = 40 m. Rectangle from 4.0 s to 10 s: 6.0 s × 20 m s⁻¹ = 120 m. Total displacement = 40 m + 120 m = 160 m.

questions.q: The graph shows how the position x of a body moving along a straight line varies with time t. O, A, B and C are points on the graph. Which statement about the motion is correct?
options: During BC the body slows down, because the line slopes downwards.
During AB the body moves at a constant velocity of 6 m s⁻¹.
During BC the body moves at constant velocity in the negative direction.
During OA the acceleration is greatest, because the body moves fastest then.
optionWhy: A student who reads the graph as a picture of the motion picks this. BC is a straight line, so its gradient, the velocity, is constant at −2 m s⁻¹: the body moves at a steady 2 m s⁻¹ in the negative direction. Only a curved section would show a changing speed.

A student who reads the height of the graph as the velocity picks this. The height of a position–time graph is the position: during AB the position stays at 6 m, so the gradient, and hence the velocity, is zero and the body is at rest.

Velocity is the gradient of a position–time graph. BC is a straight line, so its gradient is constant; the gradient is negative, (−2 − 6) m ÷ (8 − 4) s = −2 m s⁻¹, so the body moves steadily in the negative direction, passing through x = 0 at t = 7 s.

A student who links a large speed to a large acceleration picks this. During OA the body does move fastest, at 3 m s⁻¹, but OA is a straight line, so the velocity is constant and the acceleration is zero.
questions.explain: Velocity is the gradient of a position–time graph. BC is a straight line, so its gradient is constant; the gradient is negative, (−2 − 6) m ÷ (8 − 4) s = −2 m s⁻¹, so the body moves steadily in the negative direction, passing through x = 0 at t = 7 s.

questions.q: A runner moves along a straight track. Observer A measures her position from a marker M, taking the direction in which she first runs as positive. Observer B measures her position from a marker N, which is 15 m from M in the positive direction, and takes the same direction as positive. According to observer A, the runner starts at +25 m, runs to +95 m, turns round, runs back to +5.0 m and stops. What is the displacement of the runner according to observer B?
optionWhy: A student who takes displacement to be the final position measured from the origin gives the runner's final position according to B, (5.0 − 15) m = −10 m. Displacement is the change in position, final minus initial, and the runner started at +10 m according to B.

A student who treats displacement as a length that cannot be negative drops the sign. The runner finishes 20 m on the negative side of where she started, so her displacement is −20 m whichever observer measures it.

Displacement is the change in position. According to B the runner starts at +10 m and finishes at −10 m, so her displacement is (−10) − (+10) = −20 m, the same as A finds: moving the origin shifts every position by the same amount and leaves the change unaltered.
A student who equates displacement with distance adds the two legs: 70 m out and 90 m back. That is the distance travelled; the displacement depends only on the start and finish positions.
questions.explain: Displacement is the change in position. According to B the runner starts at +10 m and finishes at −10 m, so her displacement is (−10) − (+10) = −20 m, the same as A finds: moving the origin shifts every position by the same amount and leaves the change unaltered.
questions.working: According to B, positions are 15 m less than according to A: the runner starts at (25 − 15) m = +10 m and finishes at (5.0 − 15) m = −10 m. Displacement = x(final) − x(initial) = (−10 m) − (+10 m) = −20 m. This equals A's value, (5.0 − 25) m = −20 m: displacement is a change in position, so it does not depend on where the origin is placed. (Distance travelled = 70 m + 90 m = 160 m.)

questions.q: A ball is thrown vertically upwards from a point 1.20 m above the ground. It rises to a maximum height of 6.70 m above the ground, falls, and is caught at a point 1.70 m above the ground. Upwards is taken as positive. What are the distance travelled by the ball and its displacement, from the throw to the catch?
optionWhy: A student who takes displacement and distance to be the same quantity gives 10.5 m for both. The path length is 10.5 m, but the ball finishes only 0.50 m above where it started, so its displacement is +0.50 m.
A student who confuses displacement with position gives the final height above the ground, 1.70 m. Displacement is measured from the starting position, 1.20 m above the ground, not from the ground.

A student who uses 'distance' in its everyday sense, the separation of the start and finish points, and 'displacement' for the length of the path, has the two quantities the wrong way round. In physics the distance is the path length, 10.5 m, and the displacement is the change in position, +0.50 m.
Distance is the length of the path: 5.50 m up then 5.00 m down, 10.5 m in total. Displacement is the change in position, final minus initial: 1.70 m − 1.20 m = +0.50 m, upwards.
questions.explain: Distance is the length of the path: 5.50 m up then 5.00 m down, 10.5 m in total. Displacement is the change in position, final minus initial: 1.70 m − 1.20 m = +0.50 m, upwards.
questions.working: Distance travelled = length of path = (6.70 − 1.20) m up + (6.70 − 1.70) m down = 5.50 m + 5.00 m = 10.5 m. Displacement = change in position = (1.70 − 1.20) m = +0.50 m (0.50 m upwards).

questions.q: The graph shows how the velocity of a body moving along a straight line varies with time. The dashed line is the tangent to the curve at P, where t = 2.0 s. What is the instantaneous acceleration of the body at t = 2.0 s?
optionWhy: The instantaneous acceleration is the gradient of the tangent at P. Reading the two marked points on the tangent, (12 − 2.0) m s⁻¹ ÷ (5.0 − 0) s = 2.0 m s⁻².

A student who calculates a = v/t with the velocity and time at P, 6.0 m s⁻¹ ÷ 2.0 s, picks this. That is the gradient of the chord from the origin to P, the AVERAGE acceleration over the first 2.0 s. The curve is flattening, so the acceleration at t = 2.0 s is less than that average.
A student who reads the height of the graph at P as the acceleration picks this. The height of a velocity–time graph is a velocity, 6.0 m s⁻¹; the acceleration is the gradient of the tangent.

A student who divides the change in time by the change in velocity, 5.0 s ÷ 10 m s⁻¹, picks this. A gradient is the change in the vertical-axis quantity divided by the change in the horizontal-axis quantity: Δv/Δt, giving units m s⁻².
questions.explain: The instantaneous acceleration is the gradient of the tangent at P. Reading the two marked points on the tangent, (12 − 2.0) m s⁻¹ ÷ (5.0 − 0) s = 2.0 m s⁻².
questions.working: Instantaneous acceleration = gradient of the tangent to the velocity–time graph at P. The tangent passes through (0, 2.0 m s⁻¹) and (5.0 s, 12 m s⁻¹): a = (12 − 2.0) m s⁻¹ ÷ (5.0 − 0) s = 10 m s⁻¹ ÷ 5.0 s = 2.0 m s⁻². (For comparison, the average acceleration over the first 2.0 s is 6.0 m s⁻¹ ÷ 2.0 s = 3.0 m s⁻².)

questions.q: A stone is released from rest and falls 5.00 m. Fluid resistance is negligible. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². What is the speed of the stone when it has fallen 5.00 m?
optionWhy: A student who stops at v² = u² + 2as = 98.0 has found the square of the speed, in m² s⁻². Taking the square root gives v = 9.90 m s⁻¹.
With downwards positive, v² = u² + 2as = 0 + 2 × 9.8 × 5.00 = 98.0 m² s⁻², so v = √98.0 = 9.90 m s⁻¹.
A student who leaves out the ½ in s = ½gt² finds t = √(5.00/9.8) = 0.714 s and then v = gt = 7.00 m s⁻¹. With the ½, t = √(2 × 5.00/9.8) = 1.01 s and v = 9.90 m s⁻¹.
A student who divides the distance by the time of fall, 5.00 m ÷ 1.01 s, finds the AVERAGE speed during the fall. The stone accelerates uniformly from rest, so its final speed is twice this average.
questions.explain: With downwards positive, v² = u² + 2as = 0 + 2 × 9.8 × 5.00 = 98.0 m² s⁻², so v = √98.0 = 9.90 m s⁻¹.
questions.working: Take downwards as positive: u = 0, s = 5.00 m, a = 9.8 m s⁻². v² = u² + 2as = 0 + 2(9.8 m s⁻²)(5.00 m) = 98.0 m² s⁻², so v = √98.0 = 9.90 m s⁻¹.

questions.q: The graph shows how the velocity of a body moving along a straight line varies with time. What is the displacement of the body between t = 0 and t = 4.0 s?
optionWhy: Read u = +12 m s⁻¹ and v = −4.0 m s⁻¹ at t = 4.0 s from the graph. With uniform acceleration, s = ((u + v)/2)t = (12 − 4.0)/2 × 4.0 = 16 m. Equivalently, the area above the axis (+18 m) plus the area below it (−2.0 m) gives +16 m.

A student who treats displacement as the distance travelled adds the two areas without regard to sign: 18 m + 2.0 m = 20 m. After t = 3.0 s the velocity is negative, so the body moves back and that 2.0 m reduces the displacement.
A student who enters the final velocity as +4.0 m s⁻¹, ignoring its sign, calculates ((12 + 4.0)/2) × 4.0 = 32 m. The graph shows v = −4.0 m s⁻¹ at 4.0 s; the sign must be carried into the equation.
A student who finds a = −4.0 m s⁻² correctly but uses s = ut + ½at without squaring the time gets 48 − 8 = 40 m. With t² the second term is ½ × (−4.0) × 16 = −32 m, giving 16 m.
questions.explain: Read u = +12 m s⁻¹ and v = −4.0 m s⁻¹ at t = 4.0 s from the graph. With uniform acceleration, s = ((u + v)/2)t = (12 − 4.0)/2 × 4.0 = 16 m. Equivalently, the area above the axis (+18 m) plus the area below it (−2.0 m) gives +16 m.
questions.working: From the graph, u = +12 m s⁻¹, v = −4.0 m s⁻¹ at t = 4.0 s. The line is straight, so the acceleration is uniform and s = ((u + v)/2)t = ((12 + (−4.0))/2) × 4.0 = 4.0 m s⁻¹ × 4.0 s = 16 m. Check by areas: +½ × 3.0 × 12 = +18 m above the axis, −½ × 1.0 × 4.0 = −2.0 m below it, total +16 m. (a = (−4.0 − 12)/4.0 = −4.0 m s⁻²; s = ut + ½at² = 48 − 32 = 16 m.)

questions.q: A car starts from rest and moves along a straight road. Its acceleration is greatest at the start and decreases continuously, falling quickly at first and then more slowly, but stays positive, until the car reaches 20 m s⁻¹ at t = 10 s. Which gives the distance travelled by the car in these 10 s?
options: Between 100 m and 200 m, since its speed rises fastest early on
Exactly 100 m, as its average velocity is (0 + 20)/2 m s⁻¹
Exactly 200 m, as it moves at 20 m s⁻¹ for the whole 10 s
Less than 100 m, as the curve of its velocity–time graph bends upwards
optionWhy: The velocity–time graph rises steeply and then flattens, so it lies above the straight line from (0, 0) to (10 s, 20 m s⁻¹), whose area is 100 m. The velocity stays below 20 m s⁻¹ until t = 10 s, so the area is also less than 20 × 10 = 200 m.
A student who uses (u + v)/2 for any motion gets 10 m s⁻¹ × 10 s. That average holds only for uniform acceleration. Here the car gains speed early, so its average velocity is more than 10 m s⁻¹.

A student who uses distance = speed × time with the final speed treats the car as moving at 20 m s⁻¹ throughout. It started from rest and was slower than 20 m s⁻¹ until t = 10 s, so it travelled less than 200 m.

A student who copies the shape of the acceleration–time graph, which falls steeply and then levels off (bending upwards), onto the velocity–time graph draws a curve that rises slowly at first and lies below the straight line to (10 s, 20 m s⁻¹), giving less than 100 m. The acceleration is the gradient of the velocity–time graph: it is greatest at the start, so the graph is steepest at first and curves downwards, lying above that line, and the distance exceeds 100 m.
questions.explain: The velocity–time graph rises steeply and then flattens, so it lies above the straight line from (0, 0) to (10 s, 20 m s⁻¹), whose area is 100 m. The velocity stays below 20 m s⁻¹ until t = 10 s, so the area is also less than 20 × 10 = 200 m.
questions.working: Displacement = area under the velocity–time graph. Uniform acceleration from 0 to 20 m s⁻¹ in 10 s would give a straight line with area ½ × 10 s × 20 m s⁻¹ = 100 m. With the acceleration greatest at the start and decreasing, the graph is a curve that rises steeply then flattens, lying above that straight line, so the area exceeds 100 m. The acceleration is positive throughout, so the velocity is below 20 m s⁻¹ before t = 10 s and the area is less than 20 m s⁻¹ × 10 s = 200 m. So 100 m < distance < 200 m.

questions.q: A ball is kicked from level ground at 20.0 m s⁻¹ at 30.0° above the horizontal. Fluid resistance is negligible. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². What is the maximum height reached by the ball?
optionWhy: A student who swaps sin and cos uses 20.0 cos 30.0° = 17.3 m s⁻¹ as the vertical component. With θ measured from the horizontal, the vertical component is the one opposite θ, u sin θ.

A student who does not resolve uses the launch speed, 20.0 m s⁻¹, in the vertical equation. Only the vertical component, 10.0 m s⁻¹, is reduced to zero by gravity; the horizontal component is unaffected.
The vertical component of the launch velocity is 20.0 sin 30.0° = 10.0 m s⁻¹. At the maximum height the vertical velocity is zero, so 0 = 10.0² − 2 × 9.8 × h, giving h = 5.10 m.

A student who multiplies the initial vertical speed, 10.0 m s⁻¹, by the time to the top, 1.02 s, treats the vertical speed as constant. It falls steadily to zero, so the average vertical speed, 5.0 m s⁻¹, must be used.
questions.explain: The vertical component of the launch velocity is 20.0 sin 30.0° = 10.0 m s⁻¹. At the maximum height the vertical velocity is zero, so 0 = 10.0² − 2 × 9.8 × h, giving h = 5.10 m.
questions.working: Vertical component of launch velocity: u_y = u sin θ = 20.0 × sin 30.0° = 10.0 m s⁻¹ (upwards positive). At maximum height v_y = 0: v_y² = u_y² − 2gh, so h = u_y²/(2g) = (10.0 m s⁻¹)² / (2 × 9.8 m s⁻²) = 5.10 m.

questions.q: A stone is thrown from the top of a cliff at 15.0 m s⁻¹ at 30.0° below the horizontal. It lands in the sea 40.0 m below the point of release. Fluid resistance is negligible. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². How long after release does the stone reach the sea?
optionWhy: The initial vertical velocity is 15.0 sin 30.0° = 7.50 m s⁻¹ downwards. With downwards positive, 40.0 = 7.50t + 4.9t², whose positive root is t = 2.19 s.

A student who treats the stone as launched horizontally sets the initial vertical velocity to zero: 40.0 = 4.9t², t = 2.86 s. A launch below the horizontal has a downward vertical component, 7.50 m s⁻¹, which shortens the fall.
A student who swaps sin and cos uses 15.0 cos 30.0° = 13.0 m s⁻¹ as the vertical component, giving 1.82 s. With θ measured from the horizontal, the vertical component is u sin θ = 7.50 m s⁻¹.

A student who enters the launch component as +7.50 m s⁻¹ while taking upwards as positive (with s = −40.0 m and a = −9.8 m s⁻²) treats the stone as if it were thrown upwards, giving 3.72 s. The component is downwards, so with upwards positive it is −7.50 m s⁻¹.
questions.explain: The initial vertical velocity is 15.0 sin 30.0° = 7.50 m s⁻¹ downwards. With downwards positive, 40.0 = 7.50t + 4.9t², whose positive root is t = 2.19 s.

questions.q: The diagram shows the path of a ball launched from O over level ground. Fluid resistance is negligible. P, Q and R are three points on the path. Which statement about the ball is correct?
options: The horizontal component of velocity at R is less than at P.
At P the acceleration of the ball is directed along the path, towards Q.
At Q the velocity is zero, as the ball is momentarily at rest.
The speed of the ball at R is equal to the speed of the ball at P.
optionWhy: A student who imagines the ball's forward motion being used up picks this. With fluid resistance negligible the only force is the weight, which is vertical, so the horizontal component of velocity is the same at P, Q and R.

A student who assumes the acceleration points the way the body is moving picks this. The acceleration is that of free fall, g vertically downwards, at every point of the path, including P where the ball is moving upwards and forwards.

A student who carries over 'at rest at the top' from a ball thrown straight up picks this. At Q only the vertical component of velocity is zero; the horizontal component is unchanged, so the ball is still moving horizontally at Q.

The horizontal velocity component is constant throughout, and the vertical motion is symmetrical about Q: on returning to the height of P the vertical component has the same magnitude as at P but points downwards. Equal components in magnitude give equal speeds; only the direction of the velocity differs.
questions.explain: The horizontal velocity component is constant throughout, and the vertical motion is symmetrical about Q: on returning to the height of P the vertical component has the same magnitude as at P but points downwards. Equal components in magnitude give equal speeds; only the direction of the velocity differs.

Q is the highest point of the path. P, on the rising part of the path, and R, on the falling part, lie on the same dashed horizontal line, so they are at the same height. The ground is labelled level ground.

questions.q: A shuttlecock is hit from ground level at 45° above the horizontal. Video analysis shows that it reaches its highest point 0.58 s after launch, at a horizontal distance of 3.6 m from the launch point, and lands 1.36 s after launch, 5.9 m from the launch point. Which conclusion do these data support?
options: The data must be faulty, as a projectile's path is symmetrical about its highest point.
Fluid resistance cannot explain this, as it only makes the shuttlecock move more slowly.
Fluid resistance is significant: the descent is steeper and takes longer than the ascent.
The shuttlecock falls slowly because it is light, not because of fluid resistance.
optionWhy: A student who expects a symmetrical parabola in every case rejects the data. That symmetry holds only when fluid resistance is negligible, which is not so for a shuttlecock; with fluid resistance the descent is steeper and slower.

A student who thinks fluid resistance just lowers speed without changing the path picks this. Fluid resistance changes the acceleration at every point, which changes the shape of the path and makes it lopsided.

The descent takes 1.36 − 0.58 = 0.78 s, longer than the 0.58 s ascent, and covers only 5.9 − 3.6 = 2.3 m horizontally against 3.6 m on the way up. This lopsided path is what fluid resistance produces: it reduces the horizontal velocity throughout and limits the speed of the fall.

A student who believes lighter bodies fall more slowly picks this. Without fluid resistance a light body falls with the same acceleration g as a heavy one; the shuttlecock's slow descent is caused by fluid resistance, which is large compared with its small weight.
questions.explain: The descent takes 1.36 − 0.58 = 0.78 s, longer than the 0.58 s ascent, and covers only 5.9 − 3.6 = 2.3 m horizontally against 3.6 m on the way up. This lopsided path is what fluid resistance produces: it reduces the horizontal velocity throughout and limits the speed of the fall.

questions.q: The graph shows how the velocity of a small ball released from rest varies with time. Curve P is for the ball falling in air. Line Q is for the same ball falling with fluid resistance negligible. Which statement about the graph is correct?
options: The gradient of P is less than that of Q from t = 0, since fluid resistance acts from release.
Once P becomes horizontal the ball in air is at rest, as its velocity has stopped changing.
The gradient of P increases as the ball in air speeds up, as a faster body accelerates more.
At t = 0 the gradient of P equals the gradient of Q, as the fluid resistance is zero at release.
optionWhy: A student who treats fluid resistance as a fixed force picks this. Fluid resistance depends on speed and is zero for a ball at rest, so at t = 0 the acceleration is g for both cases and the two graphs start with the same gradient; they separate only as the ball gains speed.

A student who reads a horizontal line on any motion graph as 'at rest' picks this. On a velocity–time graph a horizontal line means a constant velocity: the ball is falling steadily at its terminal speed, with zero acceleration.

A student who links a larger speed to a larger acceleration picks this. The graph shows P becoming less steep as the speed rises: the fluid resistance increases with speed, so the acceleration decreases towards zero.

The gradient of a velocity–time graph is the acceleration. At release the ball is at rest, so there is no fluid resistance and its acceleration is g, the same as for Q: P starts tangent to Q. As the ball speeds up, the fluid resistance grows, the acceleration falls and P bends away below Q, becoming horizontal at the terminal speed.
questions.explain: The gradient of a velocity–time graph is the acceleration. At release the ball is at rest, so there is no fluid resistance and its acceleration is g, the same as for Q: P starts tangent to Q. As the ball speeds up, the fluid resistance grows, the acceleration falls and P bends away below Q, becoming horizontal at the terminal speed.
questions.working: Gradient of a velocity–time graph = acceleration. At t = 0 the ball is at rest, so the fluid resistance (which depends on speed) is zero and the acceleration is g for both cases: P and Q start with the same gradient, g. As the ball in air gains speed the fluid resistance grows, the resultant force and acceleration fall, and P curves below Q, becoming horizontal (zero acceleration, constant velocity) at the terminal speed.

figure.alt: Velocity–time graph with v / m s⁻¹ on the vertical axis and t / s on the horizontal axis, for a ball released from rest. Line Q, in red, is straight, rising from the origin to the top of the graph. Curve P, in blue, also starts at the origin, at first following Q, then bending away below it and flattening to a horizontal dashed line labelled terminal speed. The origin is marked 0.

questions.q: A ball is thrown vertically upwards in air and falls back. The graph shows how its velocity varies with time, with upwards taken as positive; the ball reaches its highest point at t₁. Which statement about the motion is correct?
options: The acceleration has a larger magnitude before t₁, as the graph is steeper there.
The acceleration is g throughout, as fluid resistance changes only the speed.
At t₁ the acceleration is zero, since the velocity is zero there.
After t₁ the acceleration is positive, because the ball is speeding up.
optionWhy: The gradient of the graph is the acceleration, and the graph is steeper before t₁ than after it. While the ball rises, the fluid resistance acts downwards, with the weight, so the acceleration exceeds g in magnitude; while it falls, the fluid resistance acts upwards, against the weight, so the acceleration is less than g and falls towards zero at the terminal speed.

A student who thinks fluid resistance merely makes a body slower, leaving its acceleration at g, picks this. The gradient of the graph is not constant: it is steeper than g while the ball rises and shallower than g while it falls, because the fluid resistance adds to the weight on the way up and opposes it on the way down.

A student who thinks zero velocity means zero acceleration picks this. At t₁ the graph crosses the axis with a clearly non-zero gradient: the fluid resistance is zero at that instant, so the acceleration is exactly g downwards.

A student who reads 'speeding up' as a positive acceleration picks this. After t₁ the velocity becomes more and more negative, so the gradient, and hence the acceleration, is negative (downwards) even though the ball's speed is increasing.
questions.explain: The gradient of the graph is the acceleration, and the graph is steeper before t₁ than after it. While the ball rises, the fluid resistance acts downwards, with the weight, so the acceleration exceeds g in magnitude; while it falls, the fluid resistance acts upwards, against the weight, so the acceleration is less than g and falls towards zero at the terminal speed.

figure.alt: Velocity–time graph with v / m s⁻¹ on the vertical axis (upwards positive) and t / s on the horizontal axis, for a ball thrown vertically upwards in air. The curve starts high on the v axis and falls very steeply at first, crossing the t axis at the time marked t₁ (a red dot), then continues below the axis with an ever smaller gradient, flattening towards a horizontal dashed line labelled terminal speed. The origin is marked 0.
